title: The safe bet
hookLine: live as though actions have results; you lose nothing either way

lines: IS THERE A TEACHER YOU TRUST? NO.
cards: A village called Sālā, in the kingdom of Kosala. Its people have heard a lot of traveling teachers. One says there is another world after this one.
Another says there isn't, and that nothing you do carries forward. Each one is very sure. Then the Buddha arrives, and before he teaches anything, he asks a question.
Is there a teacher here you trust? And the villagers say, honestly: no. They've heard too many confident voices.
What would you say to a village like that?

teach.h: APAṆṆAKA: A TEACHING THAT CAN'T GO WRONG.
teach.b: The answer is in the sixtieth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings. He doesn't try to out-argue the other teachers. He offers what the sutta calls apaṇṇaka, a teaching that's sure, that can't go wrong.
Take two people. The first holds that there is no other world, that giving bears no fruit, that good and bad actions have no results. So he lives carelessly in body, speech and mind.
The second holds that actions do have results, and lives carefully. Now, says the Buddha, suppose the first is right, and there is no other world.
Even then, the wise call the careless one a person of bad conduct, here and now. And if there is another world, he loses twice. The careful one?

teach.h: IF THERE'S NO NEXT WORLD, STILL PRAISED.
teach.b: If there's no other world, the wise still praise her here and now. If there is, she gains there too.
The sutta borrows a word from dice: she has made the winning throw, and it wins both ways. Notice what he doesn't ask for. He doesn't say: believe in rebirth first, and then be good.
The question can stay open, and the way to live comes out the same. Buddhist traditions teach rebirth, and this sutta also speaks to the listener who isn't sure yet.
It asks one thing: live as if what you do has results. On an ordinary Tuesday, that might mean telling the truth on a form nobody checks. You don't have to settle the universe first.
The bet pays in this life, and again if there's another.

how: Some Buddhist teachers use this sutta when talking with people who doubt rebirth: the advice to keep the precepts and act carefully stands either way, so it can be practiced before the big questions are settled.

o: sure: a bet that can't go wrong
a doubt that can't be settled
a gamble that might go either way

games.q: inside the safe bet: tap the pairs.
p: sure, a teaching that can't go wrong
a village with no teacher it trusted
loses twice if there is another world
praised here, and gains there too

s: in this sutta the Buddha first proves rebirth, then asks people to be good
he leaves the question open: the bet comes out ahead either way.
the careful person gains even if there is no other world
the sutta says the wise praise her here and now.
the sutta borrows its image from a game of dice
the careful one has made the winning throw, and it wins both ways.

games.q: you're the Buddha, arriving at Sālā. the villagers say they trust no teacher. what do you offer them?
o: a sharper argument than the last teacher's
a way to live that comes out ahead whoever is right
a demand that they choose a side today
games.why: he offers apaṇṇaka, the sure teaching: live as though actions have results, and you lose nothing either way.

practice: Bring to mind one choice waiting for you later, a message, a purchase, a conversation, and ask it two questions slowly: if nothing I do echoes past today, is this worth doing well? And if it does echo, further than I can see?
Let the answers arrive on the out-breath, notice whether they point the same way, and rest there.

wordCard.voice: Apannaka. Sure, beyond dispute: live as though actions have results, and you come out ahead whether or not there is another world.

orig.note: Pali apaṇṇaka: sure, beyond dispute. it is the title of this sutta, and of the first tale in the Jataka collection.

carryVoice: Your line: wins either way. A careful life is praised here, and gains there too. See you tomorrow.
